hook.text: In 2000, Ralph Nader won zero states but may have cost Al Gore the presidency. Voting is a strategic game.

buildup.text: When there are three or more candidates, voting systems can produce paradoxical and unfair results.

discovery.text: The Condorcet paradox: voters can prefer A over B, B over C, and C over A—creating a cycle with no clear winner.

twist.text: This means the outcome can depend on the order candidates are compared, not just voter preferences.

climax.text: Voting isn't simply counting preferences. It's a game where the rules determine the winner as much as the votes.

punchline.text: Democracy is only as fair as its rules.

quiz.question: What is the Condorcet paradox?
options: Group preferences can cycle with no clear winner

hook.text: Kenneth Arrow proved something shocking: no voting system can satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously.

buildup.text: Arrow required: unanimity, no dictator, and independence of irrelevant alternatives. Seems reasonable.

discovery.text: With three or more candidates, every ranked voting system violates at least one of these criteria.

twist.text: This doesn't mean democracy is broken—it means every voting system involves trade-offs. No perfect method exists.

climax.text: Arrow won the Nobel Prize in 1972. His theorem remains the foundation of social choice theory.

punchline.text: Perfect fairness in voting is impossible.

quiz.question: What does Arrow's theorem prove?
options: No voting system satisfies all fairness criteria with 3+ candidates

hook.text: You love candidate C but expect they'll lose. So you vote for B to stop A from winning. That's strategic voting.

buildup.text: When voters abandon their true preference to influence the outcome, the system no longer reflects genuine preferences.

discovery.text: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem proves that every non-dictatorial voting system is susceptible to strategic voting.

twist.text: Ranked-choice voting reduces but doesn't eliminate strategic behavior. No system is fully strategy-proof.

climax.text: In the 2002 French election, Le Pen beat the Socialist because left-wing voters split between candidates.

punchline.text: Honest voting is sometimes a bad strategy.

quiz.question: What is strategic voting?
options: Voting against your preference to influence the outcome

hook.text: Why do candidates in two-party systems sound so similar? They're chasing the same voter.

buildup.text: The median voter theorem says that in majority rule elections, the candidate closest to the median wins.

discovery.text: Both candidates rationally move to the center to capture the median voter, making platforms converge.

twist.text: This model assumes single-issue voting. With multiple issues, polarization can occur despite the theorem.

climax.text: Primary elections push candidates to extremes; general elections push them back to center. A two-stage game.

punchline.text: The center voter picks the winner.

quiz.question: Why do two-party candidates converge to the center?
options: They chase the median voter to win majority

hook.text: Ross Perot won 19% of the vote in 1992. He won zero electoral votes but may have changed who won.

buildup.text: A spoiler is a candidate who can't win but takes votes from a similar candidate, changing the outcome.

discovery.text: In plurality voting (most votes wins), spoilers are devastating. A minority-supported candidate can win.

twist.text: Ranked-choice and runoff systems reduce spoiling—but they introduce new strategic problems of their own.

climax.text: The spoiler effect is why many democracies gravitate toward two-party systems over time (Duverger's law).

punchline.text: Third candidates change who wins, not how.

quiz.question: What is the spoiler effect?
options: A third candidate takes votes from a similar candidate, changing the winner

hook.text: The 2020 US presidential race cost $14 billion. Both sides felt they had to spend just to keep up.

buildup.text: Campaign spending is an arms race: if your opponent spends more, you must match or risk losing.

discovery.text: The Nash equilibrium often involves massive spending by both sides—even when the money barely moves polls.

twist.text: Most campaign money goes to undecided voters in swing states. Safe states get ignored regardless of spending.

climax.text: Spending caps and public financing try to break the arms race, but enforcement remains weak.

punchline.text: Both sides spend more. Neither side gains.

quiz.question: Why is campaign spending compared to an arms race?
options: Both sides spend more without gaining advantage

hook.text: Attack ads work. Voters say they hate negativity, but negative information sticks more than positive messages.

buildup.text: Negative campaigning is a prisoner's dilemma: both candidates prefer a clean race but fear unilateral disarmament.

discovery.text: If one goes negative and the other stays positive, the attacker gains. So both go negative. Classic defection.

twist.text: Backlash exists: too much negativity can hurt the attacker's image. The optimal level isn't maximum.

climax.text: Third-party groups (super PACs) run the dirtiest ads, giving candidates distance from the negativity.

punchline.text: Mud sticks to the thrower too.

quiz.question: Why do both candidates go negative?
options: Staying positive while the rival attacks is too risky

hook.text: In 2018, Wisconsin Republicans won 63% of legislative seats with only 45% of the total vote. How?

buildup.text: Gerrymandering draws district boundaries to concentrate opponents into few districts and spread allies across many.

discovery.text: Two techniques: 'packing' opponents into overwhelming wins and 'cracking' them into narrow losses everywhere else.

twist.text: Both parties gerrymander when they control redistricting. It's a game where the rules-maker wins the game.

climax.text: Independent commissions and algorithmic redistricting aim to remove human bias from boundary drawing.

punchline.text: Who draws the map wins the election.

quiz.question: What is 'packing' in gerrymandering?
options: Concentrating opponents into a few districts they win overwhelmingly

hook.text: Your single vote almost never decides an election. Rationally, the cost of voting exceeds the expected benefit.

buildup.text: Yet millions vote. This is the 'paradox of voting'—rational self-interest predicts nobody should bother.

discovery.text: People vote for expressive reasons: duty, identity, and the desire to feel part of a collective decision.

twist.text: If everyone reasoned this way and stayed home, a single voter would become decisive—making voting worthwhile again.

climax.text: Compulsory voting (Australia, Belgium) solves the turnout problem by eliminating the individual choice not to vote.

punchline.text: Voting is rational in ways math misses.

quiz.question: What is the paradox of voting?
options: Individual cost of voting exceeds the expected impact

hook.text: When a party leader endorses a candidate early, it signals electability—and discourages other contenders.

buildup.text: Endorsements are strategic signals: they transfer credibility and coordinate supporters around one candidate.

discovery.text: Early endorsements compress primaries. Late endorsements allow leaders to back the likely winner safely.

twist.text: Endorsing the wrong candidate is costly. Leaders risk reputation, so they wait for clearer signals.

climax.text: The 'invisible primary'—the endorsement race before votes are cast—often predicts the eventual nominee.

punchline.text: Endorsements are bets on winners.

quiz.question: Why do party leaders sometimes delay endorsements?
options: Endorsing a loser is costly to their reputation

hook.text: In Germany's parliament, no party wins a majority alone. Governing requires building a coalition of parties.

buildup.text: Coalition formation is a cooperative game: parties negotiate to split cabinet seats and policy influence.

discovery.text: Minimum winning coalition theory predicts the smallest coalition holding a majority—maximizing each member's share.

twist.text: In practice, oversized coalitions form for stability. A bare majority is fragile—one defection kills it.

climax.text: Israel's notoriously fragmented parliament produces coalitions of 5-8 parties, each extracting concessions.

punchline.text: Small parties in coalitions wield outsized power.

quiz.question: What is the minimum winning coalition?
options: The smallest group that holds a majority

hook.text: Luxembourg had 2 votes in the 1958 EU Council. Germany had 4. But Luxembourg's power was actually zero.

buildup.text: Power indices measure a player's ability to change outcomes—not their raw vote share.

discovery.text: The Banzhaf index counts how often a voter is pivotal: removing them changes the result from winning to losing.

twist.text: A player with 49% of votes can have zero power if 51% always votes together. Size isn't power.

climax.text: Power indices redesigned the EU voting system to better reflect population and actual influence.

punchline.text: Power is about pivotality, not size.

quiz.question: What does the Banzhaf power index measure?
options: How often a voter is pivotal to the outcome

hook.text: A party with just 5% of seats can decide which major party governs. That's a kingmaker.

buildup.text: When two large parties are close in seats, a small party that joins either side becomes decisive.

discovery.text: Kingmakers extract disproportionate policy concessions. Their vote share is small, but their leverage is huge.

twist.text: Playing kingmaker is risky: if voters punish you for propping up an unpopular government, you lose next time.

climax.text: The UK's Liberal Democrats played kingmaker in 2010, joining the Conservatives—and lost over half their seats in 2015.

punchline.text: Kingmakers reign briefly but fall hard.

quiz.question: What makes a party a 'kingmaker'?
options: Being able to decide which major party forms government

hook.text: The US president can veto any bill. The Senate can block nominations. Veto power is everywhere in politics.

buildup.text: A veto player is any actor whose agreement is needed to change the status quo.

discovery.text: More veto players mean more policy stability—but also more gridlock. Change becomes harder to achieve.

twist.text: Skilled politicians bypass veto players using executive orders, budget riders, and procedural maneuvers.

climax.text: George Tsebelis showed that the number and ideological distance of veto players predicts policy stability.

punchline.text: One 'no' can outweigh a hundred 'yes' votes.

quiz.question: What effect do more veto players have?

hook.text: A senator proposes a bill. Others amend it, horse-trade, and add pork barrel projects. Legislation is bargaining.

buildup.text: Baron and Ferejohn modeled legislatures as bargaining games: one member proposes, others vote to accept or reject.

discovery.text: The proposer has enormous power—they design the bill. Others accept if it's better than rejecting and waiting.

twist.text: Agenda control—deciding what gets voted on—is often more powerful than the vote itself.

climax.text: The Speaker of the US House controls the floor agenda. That procedural power shapes every law that passes.

punchline.text: Who sets the menu picks the meal.

quiz.question: Why is agenda control powerful in legislatures?
options: Deciding what's voted on shapes outcomes more than voting itself

hook.text: For 45 years, the US and USSR avoided nuclear war through a strategy called mutually assured destruction.

buildup.text: Deterrence works by threatening retaliation so devastating that attack becomes irrational.

discovery.text: The key requirement: second-strike capability. You must be able to retaliate even after being attacked first.

twist.text: Deterrence requires appearing slightly irrational—enemies must believe you'd actually follow through on destruction.

climax.text: Schelling called this the 'threat that leaves something to chance'—even leaders can't fully control escalation.

punchline.text: Peace through the promise of destruction.

quiz.question: What is essential for nuclear deterrence to work?

hook.text: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy pushed the world to the edge of nuclear war—and blinked last.

buildup.text: Brinkmanship is deliberately escalating a crisis to force the other side to concede. Pure game of chicken.

discovery.text: The side that appears more willing to tolerate disaster gains leverage. Credible recklessness is power.

twist.text: But brinkmanship risks catastrophic miscalculation. Both sides might refuse to back down.

climax.text: Schelling argued that brinkmanship works by creating a risk neither side fully controls.

punchline.text: The brink is where leverage lives.

quiz.question: What game does brinkmanship most resemble?

hook.text: The US and USSR each had 30,000 nuclear warheads. Arms control treaties reduced both arsenals by 80%.

buildup.text: Arms control agreements are binding commitments to escape a prisoner's dilemma: both sides disarm together.

discovery.text: Verification is everything. Without inspections, each side fears the other is secretly cheating.

twist.text: Treaties also serve as focal points: they define 'acceptable' arsenals and prevent misinterpretation of intent.

climax.text: The collapse of the INF Treaty in 2019 shows how trust erosion can unravel decades of cooperation.

punchline.text: Trust but verify—the arms control motto.

quiz.question: What makes arms control treaties effective?

hook.text: The US sanctioned Iran to stop its nuclear program. Iran's economy suffered—but it kept enriching uranium.

buildup.text: Sanctions are costly signals: 'We'll hurt our own trade to punish you.' The pain must exceed the target's gain.

discovery.text: For sanctions to work, they must impose costs greater than the value the target places on the banned behavior.

twist.text: Sanctions often hurt civilians more than leaders. Autocrats can redirect resources to themselves.

climax.text: Smart sanctions target leaders' assets and allies directly—freezing bank accounts, banning travel.

punchline.text: Sanctions punish, but rarely persuade alone.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of broad economic sanctions?
options: They hurt civilians more than decision-makers

hook.text: NATO started with 12 members in 1949. Today it has 31. Why do nations form military alliances?

buildup.text: Alliances are commitment devices: an attack on one triggers a response from all, raising the cost of aggression.

discovery.text: Burden-sharing is the alliance's dilemma: each member wants others to spend more on defense.

twist.text: The US pays a disproportionate share of NATO's costs. Smaller members free-ride on American protection.

climax.text: Alliances work when the commitment is credible. Would the US really risk war to defend a small ally?

punchline.text: Alliances deter when doubt is minimal.

quiz.question: What is the free-rider problem in alliances?
options: Smaller members rely on larger ones to bear defense costs

hook.text: The US splits power among Congress, the President, and the courts. Why not let one body do everything?

buildup.text: Separation of powers creates multiple veto players, making it hard for any faction to seize total control.

discovery.text: In game theory, this is commitment through institutional design: leaders bind their own future power.

twist.text: The downside: gridlock. When branches disagree, government can't act—even when action is urgent.

climax.text: Parliamentary systems trade gridlock risk for efficiency: the executive and legislature are fused.

punchline.text: Freedom's price is occasional paralysis.

quiz.question: What is the game-theoretic purpose of separation of powers?
options: Preventing any faction from seizing total control

hook.text: Should states set their own tax rates? In the US, states compete to attract businesses with lower taxes.

buildup.text: Fiscal competition between states is a prisoner's dilemma: all cut taxes, all lose revenue, nobody wins.

discovery.text: This 'race to the bottom' in taxes and regulations drives down public services that businesses also need.

twist.text: But federalism also enables experimentation. States can try policies others copy if they work.

climax.text: The balance between competition and coordination defines effective federal design.

punchline.text: Competing states can race to the bottom.

quiz.question: What happens when states compete to lower taxes?
options: A race to the bottom in public services

hook.text: A constitution is a set of rules written before the game begins. It shapes every political move that follows.

buildup.text: Designers must anticipate strategic behavior: how will future politicians exploit loopholes or bend rules?

discovery.text: Behind the 'veil of ignorance'—not knowing your future position—people design fairer institutions.

twist.text: But constitution-makers aren't ignorant. They often design rules that favor their current position.

climax.text: Amendability is key: too rigid and society can't adapt; too flexible and leaders rewrite rules at will.

punchline.text: Constitutions are games about games.

quiz.question: What does the 'veil of ignorance' help achieve?

hook.text: US presidents serve a maximum of two terms. Without limits, incumbents might never leave power.

buildup.text: Term limits solve a commitment problem: leaders promise to step down, but once powerful, why would they?

discovery.text: Fixed terms create enforceable rotation. The rule binds leaders before they gain the power to ignore it.

twist.text: But term limits waste experienced leaders and make lame ducks of outgoing officials who can't be reelected.

climax.text: Russia and China modified term limits to extend leaders' rule—showing how fragile the constraint can be.

punchline.text: Power concedes nothing without structure.

quiz.question: What problem do term limits solve?

hook.text: New Zealand switched from first-past-the-post to proportional representation in 1996. Politics transformed overnight.

buildup.text: Electoral systems shape party structure. Plurality systems create two parties; proportional ones create many.

discovery.text: Each system trades off representativeness against governability. More parties mean more voices but harder coalitions.

twist.text: No system is neutral. Every rule advantages some groups and disadvantages others. Design is political.

climax.text: Countries rarely change systems because those in power were elected by the current rules.

punchline.text: The rules decide who can win.

quiz.question: Why do countries rarely change their electoral systems?
options: Those in power benefit from the current system

hook.text: If you control which options are voted on, you can manipulate the outcome—even if voting is fair.

buildup.text: Agenda setters choose the order of votes. By pairing options strategically, they steer results.

discovery.text: The Condorcet paradox makes this possible: with cycling preferences, the last option standing depends on sequence.

twist.text: Committee chairs in legislatures wield this power daily—choosing what reaches the floor and what dies.

climax.text: Riker's 'heresthetics' studies how politicians restructure choices to change outcomes without changing preferences.

punchline.text: Control the question and you control the answer.

quiz.question: How does agenda setting manipulate outcomes?
options: By controlling the order and pairing of votes

hook.text: Senator A votes for Senator B's highway bill. In return, B votes for A's school bill. Both win.

buildup.text: Log-rolling is vote trading: legislators swap support on issues they care less about for issues they care more about.

discovery.text: It can improve welfare by passing bills that benefit minorities intensely but leave the majority indifferent.

twist.text: But log-rolling can also pass bills that most voters oppose—bloating budgets as everyone adds their pet project.

climax.text: Omnibus bills bundle dozens of unrelated provisions. Each lawmaker supports the whole package for one provision.

punchline.text: Trade votes and everyone gets something.

quiz.question: What is the downside of log-rolling?
options: It can pass bills most voters oppose

hook.text: After the 2020 census, both US parties spent millions on redistricting—drawing maps to maximize seats.

buildup.text: Redistricting is a game within a game: the outcome of the map-drawing process determines future elections.

discovery.text: Algorithms can now generate thousands of maps, optimizing partisan advantage while appearing neutral.

twist.text: Courts strike down extreme gerrymanders, but the Supreme Court ruled partisan gerrymandering isn't justiciable.

climax.text: Some states use citizen commissions, but even 'neutral' rules embed assumptions favoring certain outcomes.

punchline.text: Every map is a political argument.

quiz.question: What role do algorithms play in modern redistricting?
options: They optimize partisan advantage while appearing neutral

hook.text: Strom Thurmond spoke for 24 hours and 18 minutes to block the Civil Rights Act of 1957. That's a filibuster.

buildup.text: The filibuster lets a minority block legislation in the US Senate. It raises the threshold from 51 to 60 votes.

discovery.text: In game theory, the filibuster gives minorities a veto—changing the game from majority rule to supermajority rule.

twist.text: The modern filibuster requires no speaking. Senators merely signal intent, and bills are silently blocked.

climax.text: Both parties use and condemn the filibuster depending on whether they're in the majority or minority.

punchline.text: A minority veto hiding in plain sight.

quiz.question: How does the filibuster change the legislative game?
options: It raises the threshold from majority to supermajority

hook.text: Russia's Internet Research Agency created fake social media accounts to influence the 2016 US election.

buildup.text: Information warfare manipulates beliefs, not votes directly. If you change what people think, you change how they vote.

discovery.text: Game theory models propaganda as a cheap talk game: senders have incentives to lie, receivers must assess credibility.

twist.text: Flooding the information space with noise can be as effective as propaganda. Confusion breeds disengagement.

climax.text: Democratic resilience requires media literacy: citizens who can distinguish signals from strategic noise.

punchline.text: Controlling the narrative controls the vote.

quiz.question: How does information warfare affect elections?
options: It manipulates beliefs to change voting behavior
